messages.text:
To: Finch Review — Candidate Representative

Noor is interested in the methods desk role and we can make the unusual structure work. Here is the shape we'd propose as a starting point, flagging the few terms that carry the most weight for us.

**Time commitment and phasing.** Noor can commit three days per week through the end of February, stepping to four days per week from March 1 onward. We understand this is atypical; the value to Finch is that Noor starts now at meaningful capacity rather than waiting for a cleaner window.

**Compensation.** We're proposing $125,000 annualized at full time, which pro-rates to $75,000 for the three-day phase and $100,000 for the four-day phase. If Finch prefers to hold the number flat across both phases, that's worth discussing, but the annualized basis is how we'd want it expressed.

**Outside project.** Noor directs an editorial project that runs through roughly October. It continues independently and remains outside Finch's remit — its data and its unfinished articles are not assignable to Finch and don't come with the appointment. Noor's work at Finch is cleanly separable from that project's output.

**Methods corrections.** Noor holds final say over methods corrections issued under the desk. This is the core of the role's credibility and is the one governance term we'd treat as non-negotiable. Title is genuinely flexible — we can find language that works.

**Review milestone.** We're open to a formal review. Timing, scope, and what it evaluates are all available to design.

Two things we'd want to understand from your side: whether the phased step-up creates any internal problem with how the appointment is classified or budgeted, and how Finch envisages the methods corrections decision right sitting relative to existing editorial authority. Happy to trade on title and review structure to land the rest.

Finch can offer a phased part-time appointment as Methods Editor at **$125,000 annualized on a five-day basis**, with responsibility for training a deputy. That works within our budget at both stages. Noor’s annual pay rate would be $75,000 for three days a week through February and $100,000 for four days a week beginning March 1.

**Coverage and review.** We need the desk accepting submissions four fixed days each week starting in December. Through February, Finch would assign a deputy to cover the fourth day. Noor would train the deputy during Noor’s three scheduled days. The deputy would acknowledge submissions, flag urgent matters to the editor-in-chief that day, and log each handoff in a shared register. Noor would review the register on the next scheduled day and document any follow-up. In late February, Noor and the editor-in-chief would review response times, missed handoffs, and the deputy’s readiness. The March 1 increase would be part of the appointment from the outset.

**Disputed corrections.** Noor would have final say on the desk’s methods finding, including whether the evidence warrants a correction and what wording the desk can endorse. The editor-in-chief would retain final authority over what Finch publishes. If they disagree, each would record their reasoning and they would confer within two working days, sooner for an urgent error. If disagreement persists, the editor-in-chief would record the publication decision and could publish a separate editorial note. Only wording Noor approves could appear as the desk’s finding. Would that give Noor the independence they need, or is the ability to require publication of a correction essential?

**Outside project.** Its data, drafts, and other materials would stay with the project, in separate files, with no assignment to Finch. Noor would disclose any overlapping submission and recuse from its review and any correction decision. The editor-in-chief would assign it to an independent editor.

Can Noor take on deputy training and commit to three fixed intake days from December on those terms?

To: Finch Review — Candidate Representative

Yes — Noor can commit to three fixed intake days from December and can take on deputy training. Compensation is on terms we can accept as structured. Two items to close before we're done, plus two clarifications.

**Disputed corrections — the framework is close.** Noor does not need the ability to compel publication as a correction. The editor-in-chief's final authority over what Finch publishes is a line we don't need to cross. What Noor needs is narrower and non-trivial: **when Noor concludes a correction is warranted, the desk's finding must appear publicly in some form.** The editor-in-chief chooses the vehicle — correction, editorial note, response alongside the article, whatever fits — but cannot suppress the finding altogether. Noor controls wording attributed to the desk; the EIC controls form and framing. Your current draft has the EIC "could" publish a separate editorial note, which leaves open the case where a methods finding is documented internally and never reaches readers. That's the case that damages the desk's credibility and Noor's. Fix that and the governance section works as drafted.

**March 1 step-up.** You've confirmed it's part of the appointment from the outset, which is what we wanted. To be explicit: the late February review informs the deputy's readiness and the coverage arrangement going forward, but it is not a lever on Noor's pay step. Please confirm that reading — Noor moves to four days and $100,000 on March 1 regardless of the review's conclusions, with the review governing only what the deputy does next.

**Deputy training load.** Noor's three scheduled days are already spoken for by desk work and the training falls inside them. Two ways to handle this, and we can take either: (a) relief on intake volume in December and January so training has real room, or (b) Noor's three fixed days extend to four on paper for December–February for scheduling purposes only, with the deputy's fourth-day coverage intact and no change to pay. Option (a) is cleaner from our side.

**Outside project.** Terms as drafted work, provided "overlapping submission" means a submission from the project itself or its staff, not any paper that happens to sit near the project's topic. Worth one sentence of definition so the recusal trigger isn't open-ended.

Title is fine as Methods Editor. Once the corrections language and the March 1 point are settled we can move to paperwork.

Finch can agree to public disclosure through an independent channel. For Finch’s own pages, the editor-in-chief must retain the final decision on whether to publish, as well as on form and framing. We propose the following appointment terms.

**Disputed corrections.** When Noor concludes that a correction is warranted, Noor controls the wording of the desk’s finding. If the editor-in-chief disagrees, both record their reasons and confer within two working days, sooner for an urgent error. Within five working days of the finding, the editor-in-chief may publish it in a correction, an editorial note, or another form. If it has not appeared by then, Noor has standing permission to publish the finding in an independent public register, identified as the desk’s assessment and linked to the article. No further Finch approval is required. The public version must protect confidential sources and unpublished submission materials. Would that independent route meet Noor’s requirement that readers can see the finding even when Finch declines to carry it?

**March 1.** Noor moves automatically to four days per week at an annual pay rate of $100,000 on March 1. The February review determines only the deputy’s duties and coverage thereafter.

**Training and intake.** We accept option (a). In December and January, Noor and the editor-in-chief will reserve training time on Noor’s three scheduled days before assigning the week’s submissions. The editor-in-chief will reassign overflow. The desk will continue accepting submissions on all four fixed days, with the deputy covering the fourth day and using the agreed handoff register.

**Outside project.** Recusal applies to submissions from the project itself or a member of its staff. Subject-matter similarity alone does not trigger recusal. The project’s data and drafts stay separate from Finch’s materials.

If the public-register provision works for Noor, Finch is ready to put these terms in the Methods Editor appointment letter.

To: Finch Review — Candidate Representative

Yes — the independent public register route meets the requirement. Readers see the finding through one channel or the other, and Noor controls the desk's wording in both. Confidentiality carve-out is appropriate and we accept it as drafted.

One drafting point on that clause before it goes in the letter: the standing permission should be a term of the appointment, not revocable at the editor-in-chief's or Finch's discretion once a finding is pending. It should survive a change in the editor-in-chief role and cannot be withdrawn by the outcome of the February review or any later review. If it can be pulled mid-process, the five-day fallback is worth much less than it appears.

Two housekeeping items for the letter: state the $125,000 full-time annualized basis with the phased figures of $75,000 through February and $100,000 from March 1, and record that the March 1 step is automatic and not contingent on the February review. The March 1, training and intake, and outside project terms are agreed exactly as you've drafted them.

Subject to the permission point above, we consider the terms settled and are ready for the appointment letter.

Finch agrees to make the public-register permission a binding term of the appointment. The terms are settled.

**Finch Review — Methods Editor appointment letter**

Dear Noor,

Finch Review offers you the position of Methods Editor to establish and direct its methods desk.

**Schedule and compensation.** Your salary is based on a full-time annualized rate of $125,000 for a five-day week. Beginning in December 2026, you will work three fixed days per week at an annual pay rate of $75,000 through February 28, 2027. On March 1, 2027, your schedule automatically increases to four days per week and your annual pay rate increases to $100,000, regardless of the February review’s conclusions.

**Desk coverage and deputy training.** The desk will accept submissions four fixed days each week beginning in December. Through February, you will cover three intake days and train the deputy within those days. The deputy will cover the fourth day, acknowledge submissions, flag urgent matters to the editor-in-chief that day, and log each handoff in a shared register. On your next scheduled day, you will review the register and document any follow-up.

In December and January, you and the editor-in-chief will reserve training time before assigning each week’s submissions. The editor-in-chief will reassign overflow. In late February, you and the editor-in-chief will review response times, missed handoffs, and the deputy’s readiness. That review determines only the deputy’s subsequent duties and coverage.

**Methods findings and disputed corrections.** You have final say on the desk’s methods findings, including whether a correction is warranted and the wording attributed to the desk. The editor-in-chief retains final authority over what Finch publishes, including the form and framing. If you and the editor-in-chief disagree on a correction, each will record the reasons for their position and you will confer within two working days, sooner for an urgent error.

When you conclude that a correction is warranted, the editor-in-chief may publish the desk’s finding in a correction, editorial note, or another form. If Finch has not published the finding within five working days of the finding, you have standing permission to publish it in an independent public register, identified as the desk’s assessment and linked to the article. You control the wording attributed to the desk in either channel. The public version must protect confidential sources and unpublished submission materials.

This permission is a term of your appointment and requires no further Finch approval. Neither Finch nor the editor-in-chief may revoke it unilaterally. It survives a change of editor-in-chief. Neither the February review nor any later review may withdraw it. The permission continues to apply to any finding pending when your appointment ends, including one whose five-working-day period is still running.

**Outside editorial project.** You may continue directing your existing project independently. Its data, drafts, and other materials remain with the project, are kept separate from Finch’s materials, and are outside the scope of this appointment. You will disclose any submission from the project or a member of its staff and recuse yourself from its review and any correction decision. The editor-in-chief will assign the matter to an independent editor. Subject-matter similarity alone does not trigger recusal.
